item.title: [CAIXIN] Cover Story: Jensen Huang’s Exit Tests Nvidia — and the AI Boom

item.content:encoded:
Nvidia

Nvidia, the AI-computing giant co-founded by Jensen Huang, lost its CEO of 33 years when he resigned Nov. 12 after an extramarital affair. The company now faces U.S.-China chip export scrutiny, overseas sales investigations, and questions over its customer-financing model. CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO, with revenue still surging 103% year-over-year.

Megaspeed

Megaspeed is a Singapore-based data center company, formerly an overseas subsidiary of Chinese gaming firm 7Road Holdings. Transferred in March 2023 to a company controlled by Alice Huang, it became a certified Nvidia cloud partner. Its assets grew from $75 in 2022 to nearly $3 billion in 2024, drawing scrutiny over alleged diversion of restricted Nvidia chips, though it denies wrongdoing.

7Road Holdings Ltd.

According to the article, 7Road Holdings Ltd. (第七大道) is a Chinese gaming company. Its overseas subsidiary was transferred in March 2023 to a company controlled by Alice Huang and renamed Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company later involved in the Nvidia chip controversy.

Speedmatrix

Speedmatrix is a Malaysian company identified by Malaysia's trade ministry as a subsidiary of Singapore-based data center firm Megaspeed. Import records show it bought $4.13 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips and related products between May 2024 and February 2026, with the total reaching about $4.81 billion including less specific entries. Its chip purchases are under scrutiny amid alleged Nvidia chip diversion investigations.

ByteDance

According to the article, ByteDance is a heavy user of rented computing in Southeast Asia and would face stricter scrutiny under new U.S. restrictions. Its principal overseas businesses include social media and e-commerce. ByteDance has begun seeking computing capacity in North America and elsewhere to reduce its exposure to potential disruptions in Southeast Asia.

Alibaba

Alibaba is a heavy user of rented computing in Southeast Asia and faces stricter scrutiny under new U.S. export rules. CEO Eddie Wu said the rules would affect products and services planned for next year. Alibaba plans to invest heavily in its T-Head chip supply chain over two years, sourcing most additional AI chips for Alibaba Cloud from that business.

Tencent

Tencent's president Martin Lau said at a Nov. 18 earnings briefing that the next version of its Hunyuan model could take longer to release. He noted Chinese AI companies would increasingly rely on domestic chips, with new U.S. restrictions accelerating that transition.

Meta

In late October, Nvidia announced a $3 billion investment in newly issued Meta shares. Meta simultaneously announced expanded deployment of Nvidia computing and networking products, extending Nvidia's investment-and-purchasing model to another major tech company.

CoreWeave

CoreWeave became the model for Nvidia's financing arrangements in the AI boom. Nvidia began investing in CoreWeave in 2023, provided guarantees associated with leases for land, power and buildings, and agreed to purchase unsold cloud capacity. This pattern spread to other cloud providers, AI labs, and infrastructure projects.

BlackRock

According to the article, BlackRock is one of six financial institutions that partnered with Nvidia on an AI-infrastructure financing platform. The initiative was intended to initially attract more than $500 billion in outside capital, but the plan had yet to materialize.

Blackstone

Blackstone is one of six financial institutions, including BlackRock and Goldman Sachs, that partnered with Nvidia on an AI-infrastructure financing platform. The platform was initially intended to attract more than $500 billion in outside capital, though that financing plan had yet to materialize.

Goldman Sachs

According to the article, Nvidia partnered with Goldman Sachs, along with BlackRock and Blackstone, on an AI-infrastructure financing platform intended initially to attract more than $500 billion in outside capital. That financing plan had yet to materialize, according to the report.

Barclays

Barclays warned that circular transactions could inflate apparent demand and valuations when spending depended more on companies financing one another than on independent customers. This warning came amid Nvidia's growing off-balance-sheet commitments and guarantee exposure of about $550 billion, raising concerns about whether investment flows were overstating independent demand.

Morgan Stanley

Morgan Stanley said Nvidia’s near-term product pipeline limited immediate business risk, but warned that development and execution risks could rise over the next 12 to 18 months.

Citi

Citi said that weaker Nvidia control over critical supply chain resources could benefit AMD and custom chips developed by Google, Amazon and Microsoft.

AMD

AMD (超威半导体) is mentioned in the article as a potential beneficiary of Nvidia's leadership crisis. According to Citi, weaker Nvidia control over critical supply chain resources could benefit AMD and custom chips developed by Google, Amazon, and Microsoft, giving competitors an opportunity to gain ground.

Google

According to the article, Google develops custom chips that could benefit from weaker Nvidia control over critical supply chain resources, potentially gaining competitive ground alongside AMD and Amazon.

Amazon

Amazon is mentioned in the article as a developer of custom chips that could benefit from Nvidia's reduced control over critical supply chain resources, according to Citi. No further details about Amazon are provided.

Microsoft

According to the article, Microsoft is mentioned as one of the companies that could benefit from weaker Nvidia control over critical supply chain resources, alongside AMD and Google, through its development of custom chips.

Citadel Securities

Citadel Securities hosted an event in October 2025 where Jensen Huang said China has roughly half the world's AI researchers. He argued that restricting Nvidia exports would cut this large research community off from American technology, potentially accelerating development of alternatives and weakening U.S. technological dominance.

Counterpoint

Counterpoint is cited in the article regarding Nvidia's potential slower product rollout after Jensen Huang's departure. It said a slower cycle could give engineers and suppliers more time to adapt and ease research and capital spending pressure, but at the cost of slower growth.

Duan & Duan

Duan & Duan (段和段) is a law firm with a Beijing office. Its deputy director, Ding Jie, commented on Jensen Huang's resignation from Nvidia, saying it could help separate Nvidia's legal and disclosure obligations from investigations involving Huang personally, but would not shield the company from liability.

Fox News

Fox News is mentioned in the article as the outlet where President Trump gave a Nov. 19 interview in Shenzhen, during which he said he might allow sales of Nvidia's latest Blackwell chips to China in two or three years if he remained in office. This followed his earlier comments that selling less advanced chips to China was not necessarily bad.

ImportGenius

ImportGenius is a data provider that supplies import records. According to the article, its records showed that Malaysian company Speedmatrix, identified as a Megaspeed subsidiary, bought $4.13 billion worth of Nvidia AI chips and related products between May 2024 and February 2026. Including less-specific entries, the total reached about $4.81 billion.

item.title: [CAIXIN] In Depth: America’s AI Building Boom Sparks Voter Backlash
item.description:
Apple Inc.

Apple Inc. is mentioned in the article as one of the seven largest technology stocks. Following the midterm election results, these stocks, including Apple, lost a combined $1.13 trillion in market value on Nov. 5 due to concerns about tighter oversight of AI safety and infrastructure.

Microsoft Corp.
item.content:encoded:
Apple Inc.

Apple Inc. is mentioned in the article as one of the seven largest technology stocks. Following the midterm election results, these stocks, including Apple, lost a combined $1.13 trillion in market value on Nov. 5 due to concerns about tighter oversight of AI safety and infrastructure.

Microsoft Corp.

Microsoft Corp. is a major tech firm investing heavily in AI data centers, notably in Texas, and faced market losses post-midterms. It is increasing oversight of riskier neocloud projects and withdrawing from some. Microsoft pledged to reduce data center water use by 40% by 2030, using closed-loop cooling. Its commercial backlog rose 73% to $677 billion, driven by Azure commitments.

Alphabet Inc.

Alphabet Inc. is one of the seven largest tech stocks that lost a combined $1.13 trillion in market value on Nov. 5. Its Q3 capital spending rose 114% to $51.4 billion, pushing free cash flow below zero. Shares fell nearly 13% after earnings despite a doubling of cloud revenue. Alphabet also announced a $15 billion investment in Malaysian data centers.

Amazon.com Inc.

Amazon.com Inc. withdrew plans for four data centers in Virginia's Loudoun County after spending $427 million on land, paused a Texas project amid tax-break resistance, and abandoned a Maryland proposal. It reported negative third-quarter free cash flow amid heavy AI investment, with $578 billion in remaining performance obligations, mostly cloud-related.

Meta Platforms Inc.

Meta Platforms Inc. (Meta) is one of the seven largest U.S. tech stocks. It lost market value alongside peers after the November midterm elections. The company has committed substantial investment in Texas data centers. However, it reported negative third-quarter free cash flow amid heavy AI infrastructure spending.

Nvidia Corp.

Nvidia Corp. is one of the seven largest U.S. technology stocks. Following the November midterm elections, these seven companies—including Nvidia—collectively lost $1.13 trillion in market value amid concerns over stricter AI oversight and infrastructure regulation.

Tesla Inc.

Tesla Inc. is one of the seven largest technology stocks that lost a combined $1.13 trillion in market value on Nov. 5 following the midterm election results, amid concerns about tighter oversight of AI safety and infrastructure.

IREN Ltd.

IREN Ltd. is a specialized computing company involved in data center development in Texas, where it operates alongside major tech firms. The article notes that Microsoft has increased oversight of projects involving neocloud firms like IREN. The company's operations face uncertainty amid growing political pressure and stricter regulatory scrutiny on data center infrastructure in the U.S.

CoreWeave Inc.

CoreWeave Inc. is a specialized computing company involved in building AI data center infrastructure in Texas, with substantial investment commitments. The company operates alongside major tech firms in the state, which has over 649 data centers under construction or planned. Political shifts, including stricter reviews and slower approvals, may impact its U.S. expansion.

Applied Digital Corp.

Applied Digital Corp. is a specialized computing company mentioned in the article as having committed substantial investment in Texas data center projects, alongside giants like Google, Amazon, and Microsoft. The article notes Texas's business-friendly regulation attracts such firms, but doesn't provide further specific details about Applied Digital's operations or financials beyond this mention.

Goldman Sachs

According to the article, Goldman Sachs reported that the U.S. accounted for nearly half of the world’s installed data center capacity at the end of 2025 and is expected to supply about 60% of global additions through 2030. It also projected that eight major AI and cloud companies would invest $918.2 billion in 2026, up 101% from 2025, and $1.52 trillion in 2027.

Huatai Securities Co. Ltd.

Huatai Securities Co. Ltd. cited Texas’ planned data center capacity at 93.1 gigawatts (19.5 GW under construction), leading the U.S. The firm expects a new balance: construction continues at higher cost and slower pace, with local communities receiving a greater share of benefits amid stricter oversight.

China Securities Co. Ltd.

China Securities Co. Ltd. is a financial institution whose chief media and internet analyst, Yang Aili, commented on AI investment. She stated that while AI represents the future, traditional businesses must generate cash to fund it, and investors expect leading cloud providers to boost both revenue and profit margins.

SoftBank Group Corp.

SoftBank Group Corp. is reconsidering its U.S. business involving newer cloud providers (neocloud firms), potentially withdrawing from riskier projects, and looking toward other regions amid stricter oversight and political backlash over data center development.

Bridge Data Centres

Based on the article, Bridge Data Centres is a Singapore-based company. Its co-CEO, Chen Zhongjue, noted that U.S. projects take two to three years to deliver versus one to 1.5 years in Southeast Asia. He also said slower U.S. construction could create demand for alternative capacity in Asia and Australia, and that stricter rules might favor established operators.

Morgan Stanley

Morgan Stanley estimates that Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and Africa could collectively absorb 20 gigawatts of data center development displaced from the U.S. due to stricter regulations. Additionally, the firm identifies Tennessee and Louisiana as relatively accommodating U.S. markets for continued infrastructure growth amidst political and community pushback.

APCO Worldwide

APCO Worldwide is a public-affairs consultancy mentioned in the article. It expects changes to data center incentives and permitting standards to be more likely than a statewide ban. Trevor Pearson, its director of advocacy and public affairs, notes the industry can work within strict rules if they are clear, and emphasizes the need for early discussions and credible commitments with communities.

Bloomberg

Bloomberg is a global financial news and data company. In the article, it is cited as a source reporting that following the U.S. midterm elections, Microsoft increased oversight of certain neocloud projects (involving IREN, Nebius, and Nscale) and withdrew from riskier ventures, reflecting tighter industry conditions.

Cleanview

Cleanview is an energy data company referenced in the article. It reported that Texas has 649 data centers under construction or planned, the most of any U.S. state. Cleanview also estimates that recent election outcomes could affect projects representing 41% of U.S. capacity under construction or planned, while having less impact on the 56.7 gigawatts already being built nationwide.

OpenAI

OpenAI is a major AI company operating data centers in Texas, with its first flagship Stargate site located in Abilene. Its development is facing political and community pushback due to concerns over electricity, water, and infrastructure.

Nebius Group NV

Nebius Group NV is a neocloud company mentioned in the article as part of Microsoft's increased scrutiny of riskier AI infrastructure projects. Following the midterm elections, Microsoft began tightening oversight of projects involving Nebius and other newer cloud providers, reflecting broader industry caution about data center investments amid political and regulatory pressures.

Nscale PLC

Based on the article, Nscale PLC is a neocloud firm. Microsoft increased oversight of projects involving Nscale and withdrew from those it considered riskier following the midterm elections.
